text.en:
Mala had three jars. One held a stone, one held water and one looked empty but was full of air.
She could hold the stone, pour the water, and feel the air with a paper fan.
"They are all matter, but they behave differently," she said.

Everything around us is made of matter, which takes up space and has mass. Matter is usually found as solid, liquid or gas.
A solid has a fixed shape and a fixed size, like a stone or a book. A liquid has no fixed shape and takes the shape of its container, but its volume stays the same, like water or milk. A gas has no fixed shape or volume and spreads to fill the container, like air.
Solids and liquids can be seen and touched. Gases such as air can be felt as wind but cannot usually be seen.
Everything is matter. Matter is mostly a solid, a liquid or a gas.
A solid has a fixed shape. A stone stays a stone.
A liquid takes the shape of its container, like water in a glass.
A gas spreads out to fill the container, like air in a balloon.

problem.en: Water is poured from a glass into a bowl. What happens to its shape and its amount?

text.en: Water takes the shape of the bowl.

why.en: A liquid has no fixed shape.

text.en: The amount, or volume, of water stays the same.
So a liquid changes shape but not volume.

why.en: A gas would also spread out.

prompt.en: A friend says air is not matter because we cannot see it. How will you explain?

requiredIdeas.en: Air takes up space, which we can show by blowing up a balloon.
Air has mass, so it is matter.

points.en: Matter is found as solid, liquid or gas.
Solids have a fixed shape; liquids take the shape of the container; gases spread out.
Air is a gas and is matter.
